client: I've been having a really hard time since my younger sister passed away six months ago in a car accident. It's like everything I used to enjoy just feels hollow now, and I can't seem to find any reason to care about things the way I used to. I'm honestly not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I had to try something.
therapist: I'm so glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — the loss of your sister, the emptiness that's followed — is one of the most painful things a person can go through. It makes complete sense that the world feels hollow right now, and that even hope feels hard to hold onto. I'm curious, when you imagine what "caring about things again" might look like for you, does any small part of you still have a sense of what that could feel like?

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine caring about things again, it feels really distant, like trying to remember a dream. There are these tiny moments, like when I hear a song she used to love, where I feel something, but then it's immediately followed by this wave of guilt, like I shouldn't be allowed to feel okay. I guess a small part of me knows what it used to feel like, but I'm not sure I deserve to get back there.
therapist: Those small moments — like hearing her favorite song and feeling something — are actually really meaningful, and it tells me that part of you is still reaching toward life even in the middle of this grief. But I want to gently explore that guilt with you, because the idea that you "don't deserve" to feel okay is a very painful belief to be carrying — and I wonder where that comes from. When that wave of guilt hits, what does the voice in your head actually say to you?

client: The voice is pretty brutal, honestly. It says things like "she's gone and you're still here, so what gives you the right to enjoy anything" or sometimes it's more specific, like reminding me that the last time we talked I was distracted and kind of short with her, and now I can never fix that. It's like I've put myself on some kind of permanent punishment sentence and I'm not even sure I want to be talked out of it, if that makes sense.
therapist: That voice is carrying so much weight — the survivor's guilt, the unfinished moment from your last conversation — and I can hear how deeply it's dug in, almost like a part of you believes staying in pain is a way of staying loyal to her. That last part you said, about not being sure you want to be talked out of it, takes real honesty to admit, and I think it's actually one of the most important things you've shared. I'm wondering — do you think your sister, knowing you the way she did, would agree that you deserve a lifetime sentence for being distracted during one phone call?

client: No, she wouldn't, and I know that in my head, she was actually a really forgiving person and would probably be furious at me for doing this to myself. But knowing that and actually feeling it are two completely different things, and right now it just feels like a convenient argument that doesn't really touch what's going on inside. It's like I can acknowledge it intellectually but then the guilt just sits there anyway, completely unmoved.
therapist: What you're describing — knowing something in your head but not being able to feel it in your body — is actually one of the most common and frustrating parts of grief, and it doesn't mean you're broken or that healing isn't possible for you. That gap between thinking and feeling is real, and it's exactly where a lot of our work can happen over time, not by arguing the guilt away, but by slowly building a different kind of relationship with it. I'm curious — when you imagine the version of you that your sister would *want* you to become, what does that person's life look like?

client: That question actually caught me off guard a little, because when I try to picture it, I can almost see something, like someone who laughs again, who maybe has close friendships and doesn't isolate the way I've been doing. But then immediately I feel this resistance, like constructing that image is somehow a betrayal, like I'm planning a future that she doesn't get to have. It's hard to sit with that question without it turning into another reason to feel guilty.
therapist: The fact that you could actually see something — someone who laughs, who connects — even for a moment, is genuinely significant, and I don't want that to get lost under the guilt that rushed in after. What you're describing, this feeling that building a future is a betrayal, is such a common but painful part of grief, almost like you've made your suffering into a monument to her. I want to gently offer a different thought: what if living fully isn't a betrayal of your sister, but actually the most honest way of honoring someone who, by your own words, would be furious to see you suffering like this?

client: That reframe is actually kind of beautiful, and part of me wants to grab onto it, but another part of me is suspicious of how neat it sounds, like it's too clean an answer for something this messy. I've heard versions of "honor them by living well" before and it always felt like something people say to make grief more manageable for everyone around the grieving person. I don't know, maybe I'm being defensive, but I guess I'm worried that if I accept that idea too quickly, I'm just letting myself off the hook without really doing the hard work.
therapist: Your skepticism here is actually really healthy and worth respecting — you're not looking for a quick fix, you're looking for something real, and that instinct is going to serve you well in this process. I want to be clear that "honoring her by living well" isn't meant to be a tidy bow that closes the grief — it's more like a direction to move in while still carrying the mess, the guilt, the unanswered moments, all of it. I'm curious though, when you say you're worried about "letting yourself off the hook without doing the hard work" — what does that hard work actually look like to you?

client: Honestly, I'm not entirely sure what the hard work looks like, which is part of what scares me. I think it involves somehow dealing with that last conversation, maybe finding a way to say the things I never got to say to her, but I don't even know if I'm ready to go near that yet. It's like I know the wound is there but I keep my hand over it because I'm afraid of what I'll find if I actually look.
therapist: The image you just used — keeping your hand over the wound — is really telling, because it shows that some part of you already knows where the tender place is, even if you're not ready to look directly at it yet. And that's okay; readiness isn't something we force, it's something we build toward carefully, and the fact that you can name it at all is already a form of courage. When you imagine eventually finding a way to say the things you never got to say to her, what feels like it would need to be true — about you, or about this process — for that to feel even a little bit safe enough to try?

client: I think I'd need to trust that looking at it wouldn't completely undo me, like that I'd still be functional on the other side of it rather than falling apart in a way I can't come back from. I also think I'd need to feel like whatever I said to her wouldn't just disappear into nothing, that there's some way it could actually matter even though she's not here to hear it. I guess I'm asking whether you think that's even possible, or if I'm just hoping for something that therapy can't actually give me.
therapist: What you're asking is real and honest, and I want to answer it directly: yes, I do believe both of those things are possible — people do move through the hardest material without being permanently undone, and there are ways of speaking to someone we've lost that carry genuine meaning and can actually shift something inside us, even in their absence. That's not a promise that it won't hurt, but the falling apart you're afraid of and the "can't come back from" are often what the fear tells us, not what actually happens. I think the fact that you can articulate so clearly what you'd need — safety and meaning — tells me you're not as far from being ready as you might think; what would it feel like to just sit with that possibility for a little while, without having to decide anything yet?

client: Sitting with a possibility without deciding anything actually feels more manageable than I expected, like there's less pressure in that framing than I usually put on myself. I think I've been approaching this whole thing as something I need to solve or get through quickly, and the idea that I can just let something exist without acting on it right away is kind of a relief, even if it's a small one. I'm still scared, but maybe that's okay for right now.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what just shifted for you — that small relief is not nothing, it's actually a crack of light, and it came from you giving yourself a little more gentleness than you usually do. The fear being okay "for right now" is exactly the kind of permission that makes this work possible, because you're not trying to bulldoze through the grief anymore, you're starting to walk alongside it. As we close today, I'm wondering — what's one small thing you might be able to offer yourself this week, not to fix anything, but just as a gesture of the same forgiveness your sister would have so readily given you?

client: I want to say yes to that question, but my first instinct is to think of something and then immediately find a reason why it's too indulgent or too soon. Maybe I could let myself listen to one of her favorite songs without immediately shutting it down or distracting myself, just let it play and see what happens. I'm already feeling a little resistant to it though, like some part of me is saying that allowing myself to feel something good connected to her is still not something I've earned yet.
therapist: What you just described — letting the song play and seeing what happens — is actually a beautiful and perfectly sized first step, and I want to reflect back to you that you found it yourself, which matters. That voice saying you haven't "earned" it yet is the same voice we've been talking about all along, and just noticing it without automatically obeying it is itself a form of the hard work you were asking about earlier. What if this week, when that resistant voice shows up as the song plays, you just acknowledged it — "there you are" — without letting it have the final say?
